This feels slightly condescending, especially when talking about preppers. The reason society as a whole was able to make huge technological advancements was through the usage of specialization. As soon as we grew more food than we ate, some people didn't have to become farmers, which allowed for people to devote more time to another thing. Likewise, once we went from building a car from scratch to an assembly line, production increased greatly (even if many workers couldn't build a whole car).

So let's assume best case scenario; disaster strikes, but somehow we're able to maintain that standard (i.e. we're not foraging so not all of us have to be on food/water/shelter duty). Let's also go with one of the more useful examples (making a light bulb). If I knew how to make a basic light bulb before the disaster, that would be nice, true. If I didn't, am I screwed? Not really. It's unlikely that every single light bulb in existence is shattered, giving a temporary solution (using those lights) as well as a chance to study existing technology.

Would I rather get stranded with a bunch of Macguyvers or a group of highly specialized people? The specialized people. Because they have spent a lifetime learning something which may prove useful. I don't disagree with the idea that learning new things is helpful and enlightening, but I'd rather have a mechanic who knows exactly what's wrong with a vehicle (or a doctor who can quickly catalog the inventory of an abandoned hospital) than a bunch of macguyvers who jury-rig things.

Also, there was a fun discovery show that explored this concept called The Colony. It's a fun but cheesy watch on YT
